title: One country over thirty years: what the HDI and GII show and hide

readings.title: Development and gender indicators in Country R, 1995 to 2025
readings.html:
Development and gender indicators for Country R (invented data for practice). For GII, lower means less gender inequality.
Indicator199520102025
GNI per capita, PPP (US$)6,00011,00019,000
HDI0.590.680.76
GII0.550.400.30
Maternal deaths per 100,000 births31015060
Seats in parliament held by women (%)61528
Women in paid work (%)324152
Total fertility rate4.02.92.1

Invented data for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.demand: Give the information asked for: a word or short phrase can earn the point, with no reasons needed.
parts.prompt: Identify the period, 1995 to 2010 or 2010 to 2025, in which Country R's GII fell more.

rubric.point: Names 1995 to 2010 (the GII fell by 0.15, from 0.55 to 0.40, compared with 0.10 from 2010 to 2025).

parts.sample: 1995 to 2010, when the GII fell by 0.15 (from 0.55 to 0.40); from 2010 to 2025 it fell by 0.10.

parts.label: B
parts.demand: Give the relevant characteristics: what it is like, where and how much. A name alone earns nothing.
parts.prompt: Describe the change in Country R's HDI from 1995 to 2025, using data from the table.

rubric.point: Describes a steady rise with data: from 0.59 in 1995 to 0.68 in 2010 and 0.76 in 2025.
accept: it rose in both periods, from 0.59 to 0.68 to 0.76

parts.sample: Country R's HDI rose steadily, from 0.59 in 1995 to 0.68 in 2010 and 0.76 in 2025, an increase of 0.17 over thirty years.

parts.label: C
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how the fall in maternal deaths shown in the table helps lower Country R's GII.

rubric.point: Explains that maternal deaths are part of the reproductive health dimension of the GII, so fewer deaths in childbirth (310 to 60 per 100,000 births) mean less measured disadvantage for women and a lower GII.
accept: the GII counts maternal deaths as part of reproductive health, so fewer deaths lower it
deaths in childbirth harm only women, so cutting them from 310 to 60 narrows the gap the GII measures

parts.sample: The GII measures women's disadvantage in reproductive health, empowerment and paid work, and maternal deaths are part of reproductive health. As deaths in childbirth fell from 310 to 60 per 100,000 births, women's health improved compared with men's, so this part of the index improved and the GII fell.

parts.label: D
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain ONE reason the HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone.

rubric.point: Explains that the HDI adds health (life expectancy) and education (schooling) to income, so it shows whether income becomes better lives.
accept: it adds life expectancy and schooling, so it shows more than money
it shows whether income is turned into health and education

parts.sample: The HDI is better because it adds life expectancy and years of schooling to income, so it shows whether a country turns its income into longer, better-educated lives, which GNI per capita, an average of income, cannot show.

parts.label: E
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how the rise in women's paid work shown in the table could help account for the fall in Country R's total fertility rate.

rubric.point: Explains a link: as more women work for pay (32% to 52%), they often marry later, stay in school or work longer, and each child costs more in lost earnings, so families have fewer children (4.0 to 2.1).
accept: more women in paid work means later marriage and fewer children
working women give up more income for each child, so the fertility rate falls

parts.sample: Between 1995 and 2025 the share of women in paid work rose from 32% to 52% while the total fertility rate fell from 4.0 to 2.1. Women with paid jobs often marry and have their first child later, and each child means more lost earnings, so many families choose to have fewer children.

parts.label: F
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain ONE limitation of using national data such as these to describe development within Country R.

rubric.point: Explains that national averages hide differences at a smaller scale: between regions, cities and rural areas, or groups inside Country R.
accept: one national value hides differences between regions or between cities and the countryside
the data are at the national scale, so they cannot show local or regional patterns

parts.sample: The table gives one national value for each year, so it hides differences inside Country R: the capital may have far lower maternal deaths and more women in paid work than rural regions, so an average can describe almost nobody's life.

parts.label: G
parts.demand: State the degree first (to a high, moderate or low degree), then explain why with evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the data in the table show that women and men in Country R now have equal opportunities.

rubric.point: States a degree, then supports it with data: inequality has fallen (GII 0.55 to 0.30), but the GII is still above zero and women hold only 28% of seats in parliament, so opportunities are not yet equal.
accept: to a low or moderate degree: the GII is still 0.30 and women hold only 28% of seats
to a moderate degree: big gains in health and paid work, but gaps remain in parliament

parts.sample: To a low degree. Gender inequality has fallen a great deal: the GII dropped from 0.55 to 0.30 and women in paid work rose to 52%. However, a GII of 0.30 is still well above zero, and women hold only 28% of the seats in parliament, so women still have less political power and fewer opportunities than men.
